c.tagline: West Lake serenity and Alibaba ambition, wrapped in tea hills and canals.

taxi.fareNote: Metered fares start around ¥13 for the first 3 km; most locals summon cabs and pay via Didi or Alipay/WeChat rather than hailing on the street or using cash.

emergency.note: Police 110, ambulance 120, fire 119. The 12345 city hotline handles general help; foreign-language assistance is limited, so translation apps help.

avoid.reason: Beware 'tea ceremony' and art-student scams targeting tourists around West Lake, and watch for pickpockets in dense holiday crowds.

hood_desc: The scenic heart of the city wrapped around West Lake (Xihu), with causeways, tea houses, pagodas, and Lingyin Temple nearby; best for first-timers who want Hangzhou's iconic sights within easy reach.

Downtown Hangzhou around Wulin Square and Hubin, the city's main commercial and shopping core with department stores, malls, restaurants, and a metro interchange; suits travelers who want a central, well-connected base.

A modern high-tech district on the south bank of the Qiantang River, home to riverside parks, corporate campuses, and newer residential towers; suits business travelers and those wanting quieter, contemporary surroundings.

A dense inner-city area straddling the southern end of the Grand Canal near Wulin and the Gongchen Bridge, mixing old canal-side lanes with markets and local eateries; good for travelers wanting an authentic, everyday-life feel.

The Future Sci-Tech City in Yuhang, anchored by Alibaba's campus and the Xixi Wetland, a spread-out zone of tech offices, resorts, and green space; suits business visitors and those linked to the tech scene rather than sightseers.

water.note: Stick to bottled or boiled water; avoid tap water and ice made from it.

transit.hours: Metro runs roughly 6:00 AM to 11:00 PM; city buses run from early morning until around 10-11 PM with a few late-night lines.
transit.note: Hangzhou has an extensive and still-expanding metro network (a dozen-plus lines) that reaches West Lake, the train stations, and the airport, backed by a dense bus network and ubiquitous shared bikes.
transit.pay: Pay by scanning Alipay/WeChat QR or the Hangzhou transit QR at metro gates and on buses; a rechargeable transit card and single-journey metro tokens also work. Foreign visitors typically link a card inside Alipay. Metro fares are distance-based (¥2-8).

tip.r: Tipping is not customary or expected; restaurants do not add service charge and rounding up is unnecessary.

food.name: Dongpo Pork
food.desc: Thick cubes of pork belly slow-braised in soy, rock sugar and Shaoxing wine until the fat turns to jelly. Named for the poet-governor Su Dongpo.

places.name: Lou Wai Lou
places.note: The city's most famous restaurant, lakeside since 1848; the reference version of the dish.

places.name: Zhi Wei Guan
places.note: Century-old Hangzhou house with floor-to-ceiling lake views and reliable classic cooking.

places.name: Xinzhouji
places.note: Twenty-plus-year local brand whose signature is Dongpo pork; popular with Hangzhou families.

food.name: West Lake Fish in Vinegar Gravy
food.desc: Grass carp poached until just set, then glossed in sweet-sour vinegar, sugar and ginger sauce. Delicate rather than heavy, and famously hard to cook well.

places.name: Lou Wai Lou
places.note: Widely considered the definitive version; book ahead for a window table over the water.

places.name: Zhi Wei Guan
places.note: A long-standing rival for the same dish, with easier reservations than Lou Wai Lou.

places.name: Wai Po Jia (Grandma's Home)
places.note: Affordable local chain doing solid renditions of the classics; queue-and-ticket system.

food.name: Longjing Shrimp
food.desc: River shrimp stir-fried with fresh Longjing tea leaves and a splash of the brew, so the shellfish tastes faintly of green tea and spring grass.

places.name: Lou Wai Lou
places.note: Uses genuine West Lake Longjing; best from late March when the new leaves arrive.

places.name: Meijiawu tea village restaurants
places.note: Farmhouse kitchens in the tea plantations that build whole menus around Longjing cuisine.

places.name: Zhi Wei Guan
places.note: Dependable year-round version in a comfortable central setting.

food.name: Beggar's Chicken
food.desc: A whole chicken stuffed with pork and mushrooms, wrapped in lotus leaves and clay, then baked for hours. The crust is cracked open at your table.

places.name: Lou Wai Lou
places.note: Serves the classic table-side clay-cracking presentation; order it when you book.

places.name: Zhi Wei Guan
places.note: Another old-guard house that still does the full lotus-leaf and clay preparation.

food.name: Pian Er Chuan Noodles
food.desc: Hangzhou's everyday noodle bowl: sliced pork, bamboo shoots and pickled greens in clear broth over springy wheat noodles. Cheap, fast, beloved.

places.name: Kuiyuan Guan
places.note: Noodle institution since 1867 and the dish's spiritual home; also famous for eel noodles.

places.name: Wai Po Jia
places.note: Convenient all-day option if the Kuiyuan Guan queue is out the door.

food.name: Hangzhou Dim Sum and Sweets
food.desc: The small plates that round out a Hangzhou meal: cat's-ear pasta, shrimp shaomai, lotus-root powder soup and osmanthus-scented sticky rice cake.

places.name: Zhi Wei Guan
places.note: Best known for its snack counter; order a spread of small plates rather than a set meal.

places.name: Hefang Street food lane
places.note: Restored old street packed with sweet shops, sticky rice cakes and osmanthus desserts.

food.name: West Lake Longjing Tea
food.desc: China's most famous green tea, pan-fired flat and grassy-sweet, grown on the hills behind West Lake. Best drunk within weeks of the spring picking.

places.name: Meijiawu Tea Culture Village
places.note: Six centuries of tea farming; family teahouses let you taste, watch firing and pick in season.

places.name: Longjing Village teahouses
places.note: The namesake village above the lake, with terrace teahouses looking over the plantations.

places.name: Qinghefang tea shops
places.note: Central spot to compare grades and buy tea without trekking into the hills.

food.name: Osmanthus Lotus Root Drink
food.desc: Lotus-root starch whisked with hot water into a translucent, mildly sweet gel and scented with dried osmanthus blossom. A West Lake autumn tradition.

places.name: Hefang Street stalls
places.note: Sold hot by the cup from traditional sweet shops; osmanthus is at its peak in October.

places.name: Lakeside teahouses
places.note: Many teahouses serve it as a warming alternative to tea in the cooler months.

landmarks: West Lake
A UNESCO World Heritage cultural landscape of misty waters, willow-lined causeways, and pagodas that has inspired Chinese poets and painters for a thousand years.
Leifeng Pagoda
A five-story pagoda glowing golden at dusk on West Lake's southern shore, rebuilt atop its ancient ruins and steeped in the legend of the White Snake.
Lingyin Temple
One of China's oldest and wealthiest Buddhist temples, tucked among forested hills with grottoes of ancient rock carvings leading up to it.
Six Harmonies Pagoda (Liuhe Pagoda)
A towering octagonal brick-and-timber pagoda overlooking the Qiantang River, historically built to calm the river's legendary tidal bore.
Broken Bridge (Duan Qiao)
The most romantic vantage point on West Lake, famed for the folk tale of the White Snake and for its snow-dusted views in winter.
Su Causeway
A tree-shaded, arched-bridge walkway built by poet-governor Su Dongpo that slices scenically across West Lake and is one of its ten classic views.
Beijing-Hangzhou Grand Canal
The southern terminus of the world's longest ancient canal, where centuries-old stone bridges and canal-side houses still frame everyday river life.
Hefang Street
A bustling Qing-dynasty-style pedestrian street packed with traditional shopfronts, snacks, and pharmacies, offering a vivid slice of old Hangzhou.
Xixi National Wetland Park
A vast urban wetland of waterways, reed marshes, and old fishing villages explored by hand-poled boat, a lush green escape unlike anywhere else in the city.
Baochu Pagoda
A slender Song-dynasty pagoda crowning Precious Stone Hill, offering one of the best panoramic photo spots looking down over West Lake.

train.note: Hangzhou has no international trains. Hangzhou East is the main high-speed hub, served by the Shanghai-Hangzhou, Nanjing-Hangzhou and Hangzhou-Ningbo high-speed lines - Shanghai Hongqiao is under an hour, Nanjing South about 1.5 hours, and there are through services as far as Kunming, Guangzhou and Beijing. Hangzhou (City) station and Hangzhou West handle other services, and all three are on the metro. Book on 12306 with your passport; the Shanghai shuttle runs every few minutes so you rarely need to plan ahead except at holidays.

bus.note: No international coaches serve Hangzhou. Four terminals split the traffic - the Passenger Transport Centre in the east, plus West, South and North stations - with the West station handling the mountain routes including Huangshan and Jingdezhen (about 7 hours, ¥140, departures around 09:00 and 14:20). Coaches also run to Shanghai, Suzhou, Wuzhen and Ningbo, though the train beats them on every one of those. Tickets are sold at the counters and on Chinese travel apps.

ferry.note: Hangzhou has no intercity passenger ferries; the overnight Grand Canal boat that once ran to Suzhou no longer operates. Within the city the Grand Canal water bus is a genuine and cheap way to travel between the northern districts and the centre, and there are sightseeing boats on West Lake, but neither will take you to another city.

half.name: Wuzhen
half.blurb: Canal water town of stone bridges and wooden houses on stilts, with a preserved Ming and Qing-era street grid.

half.name: Xitang
half.blurb: Water town crossed by nine rivers and over a hundred bridges, with covered corridors lining the canals.

half.name: Moganshan
half.blurb: Bamboo-forested mountain retreat dotted with early-1900s stone villas built as a colonial-era hill station.

half.name: Shaoxing
half.blurb: Canal city known for its rice wine, black-tiled bridges, and the former residence of writer Lu Xun.

full.name: Qiandao Lake
full.blurb: Reservoir of over a thousand forested islands formed by a 1959 dam, used for boat tours and fish restaurants.
